You understand and build words with prefixes and suffixes (ri-, in-, s-, dis-, stra-; -zione, -mento, -tà, -ezza; -tore, -ista, -oso, -bile; -izzare, -ificare) and you know how a new word enters the dictionary.

Florence, July. Viola has just hugged Graziella and called her “Grandma abbracciosa”. Pietro looked the word up in the dictionary and didn’t find it. He asks Bianca, who knows a lot about language.
Viola said Grandma is “abbracciosa”. It’s not in the dictionary.
It isn’t, but it’s a well-formed word. Abbraccio plus the suffix -oso. Like coraggio, coraggioso.
Exactly. A person who hugs a lot. You understand it immediately, even if nobody has ever heard it.
Then why isn’t it in the dictionary?
Because it isn’t enough for a word to be well formed. Many people have to use it. Do you remember “petaloso”?
The child who had invented a word and written to the Accademia della Crusca?
Him exactly. The Academy replied that it was a beautiful, well-formed word, but that it had to spread.

Write it. But meanwhile start using it. New words are made by walking, not by waiting.

“In-” becomes “im-” before b and p (impossibile), “il-” before l (illegale), “ir-” before r (irregolare).
Nouns in -zione, -tà and -ezza are feminine: la riproduzione, la felicità, la gentilezza. Those in -mento are masculine: il cambiamento.
“-bile” is very productive: from almost any transitive verb you can make an adjective: toccare → toccabile, guardare → guardabile, mangiare → mangiabile.
“Parasynthetic” verbs add both a prefix and an ending: bello → ab-bell-ire (to make beautiful), vecchio → in-vecchi-are (to grow old), rosso → ar-ross-ire (to blush).
5. How a new word is born

In 2016 an eight-year-old child invented the word “petaloso” (with many petals) in a school assignment. The teacher wrote to the Accademia della Crusca, and the Academy replied that it was a well-formed word, but that it enters the dictionary only if many people use it.

Come si fanno le parole nuove, secondo Bianca?

In July Davide started working at the Uffizi. Not as a restorer, not yet, but as a consultant on a project the museum had called “Uffizi to touch”, born from Mr Alberto Ricci’s letter and from the cardboard with the Lippina in relief. The aim was to make twenty masterpieces of the collection accessible to blind visitors, with touchable reproductions, audio descriptions and guided routes. The working group met twice a week in a room on the second floor, with windows over the Arno: there were an accessibility manager, two restorers, an expert in relief printing, a guide, Mr Alberto, and Davide, who was fifteen and by far the youngest. On the first day he came with his sketchbook and pencils and stayed silent for an hour. Then the manager asked him what he thought. Davide said that a touchable painting must not be a copy, but a translation. Everyone turned to look at him.

He explained what he meant with the simplest words he could find. A painting, he said, is made for the eyes: it has colours, lights, shadows, shades that fingers cannot feel. If you copy it in relief as it is, the fingers find only a tangle of lines. You have to choose. To simplify. To translate colours into different materials, as he had done with gauze for the veil and sandpaper for the rocks. To translate depth into different heights of the relief: higher what is in the foreground, lower what is in the background. “Hands read in a different way,” he said. “First they feel the whole, then the details. Eyes do the opposite.” Mr Alberto, sitting at the end of the table with his dog, nodded slowly. “The boy is right,” he said. “For twenty years they made me touch copies. I never understood anything. His cardboard I understood in five minutes.”

That evening Davide walked home along the Arno, and all the way he thought about a word he had seen a hundred times in the museum without noticing it: the “Do not touch” signs next to every painting. The works of the Uffizi were untouchable, and they had to be: the skin of the fingers leaves grease, sweat, salt, and in a few years even the hardest marble wears away. But with those signs Mr Alberto was shut out of everything. Davide opened his notebook on a bench and wrote in a column: toccare, toccabile, intoccabile, ritoccare, ritocco. Then he wrote beside it, with an arrow: “Our job is to turn the untouchable into the touchable, without touching the untouchable.” He reread the sentence and laughed to himself, because it sounded like a tongue twister. At dinner he read it to Rita. His mother, who had been restoring frescoes for twenty-five years, stayed serious. “It’s the truest sentence I’ve heard about our trade,” she said. “Write it big. One day you’ll put it on the door of your workshop.”

It was in that period that Viola invented the word. It happened on a Saturday afternoon, at the trattoria, while Graziella, who after the operation had become strangely affectionate, picked her up to let her smell Aldo’s plant. Viola threw her arms around her neck, hugged her tight and said, with the absolute seriousness of her six years: “Nonna Graziella, you’re abbracciosa.” Graziella laughed. Pietro, who was laying the tables, stopped with a fork in his hand. “What did you say?” he asked. “Abbracciosa,” Viola repeated. “Because she hugs a lot.” Pietro had never heard that word. And yet he had understood it at once, without any explanation. That evening he looked it up in the dictionary, then in three online dictionaries, then in an old dictionary that Bellini kept in the workshop. It wasn’t anywhere. Viola had invented a word. And the word worked.

The next day he told Bianca about it; since winning the competition she had become passionate about linguistics and read books on the history of Italian. Bianca listened and smiled. “It’s a well-formed word,” she said. She took a sheet of paper and broke it down like a maths problem: abbraccio, noun, plus the suffix -oso, which means “full of”. Like coraggio and coraggioso, fama and famoso, pericolo and pericoloso. “That’s why you understand it at once,” she explained. “Your cousin didn’t invent the parts. She only put together pieces that already existed, in the right way. It’s like a restoration: you don’t paint anything new, you put back together what is there.” Pietro reminded her that Viola wasn’t his cousin, she was Matei and Giulia’s daughter. Bianca shrugged. “In a kitchen like yours,” she said, “everyone is a cousin.”

Pietro, though, wasn’t satisfied. He wanted to understand the mechanism, not just an example. So Bianca prepared for him, on the back of a menu, a small table of suffixes, like the ones she had studied for the competition. With -bile, she explained, you make from a verb an adjective that means “that can be”: leggibile, mangiabile, lavabile. With -ezza and -tà, you make a noun from an adjective: gentile and gentilezza, felice and felicità. With -tore, you make from a verb the person who acts: restauratore, venditore, traduttore. And with a prefix in front everything changes: in- takes away, ri- repeats, s- reverses. Pietro looked at the table and then at the dining room of the trattoria, where Matei was clearing the tables. “So here too it’s full of words made of pieces,” he said. “Cameriere, from camera. A lavabile bottle. A sparecchiata table: s- plus apparecchiata.” Bianca applauded. “Now you’ll see them everywhere,” she promised. “It’s a disease. There’s no cure.” She was right: that night Pietro couldn’t sleep, because he kept taking apart every word that came into his head.

Then Bianca told him the story of “petaloso”. In 2016, she said, an eight-year-old boy from a village in the province of Ferrara had written in an assignment that a flower was “petaloso”, that is, full of petals. The teacher had marked the word as a mistake, but then she had thought about it and decided to write to the Accademia della Crusca, the oldest institution that studies the Italian language, founded right here in Florence in the sixteenth century. The Academy had replied with a very kind letter. It said the word was beautiful and well formed, like peloso or coraggioso. But it also said that a word doesn’t enter the dictionary because someone invents it: it enters when many people use it, in many different places. The letter ended up in the newspapers, the word became famous all over Italy, and in the end some dictionaries really added it. Pietro listened open-mouthed. “Then we can write too,” he said. Bianca nodded. “But first,” she said, “Viola has to agree. The word is hers.”

Viola agreed wholeheartedly. In fact she wanted to dictate the letter herself, with Pietro typing on the computer and Bianca checking the form. It took them a whole afternoon, in the kitchen, with Graziella listening while pretending to clean vegetables. Viola wanted to begin with “Dear Crusca”. Pietro explained that you write to an academy formally, as Karl had taught them at the letter-writing school in via Maggio. In the end the letter began like this: “Dear members of the Accademia della Crusca, my name is Viola, I am six years old and I live in Florence, in via Maggio, above a trattoria. I am writing to propose a new word: abbraccioso. It means a person who hugs a lot, like my nonna Graziella, who is not my real grandmother but is everyone’s grandmother.” Three examples of use followed, which Viola dictated without hesitating. The third was: “Ribollita is abbracciosa too, because when you eat it you feel hugged.” Graziella, at the sink, wiped her eyes with her apron.

Before sending the letter, Pietro gave it to Karl to read, since by now he was the cooperative’s official consultant for all formal letters. Karl read it carefully and changed only two things. The first: “Dear gentlemen” became “Dear academicians, women and men”, because, he said, many women worked at the Accademia della Crusca too. The second: at the end, after “Kind regards”, he added “I look forward to your kind reply”. Viola asked what that meant. Karl explained that it was an elegant formula for saying “please answer me”. Viola thought about it. Then she asked to add a line, written by her, in her crooked letters. Pietro printed the letter and gave it to her. With the red marker, Viola wrote under the signature: “PLEASE ANSWER. IT’S IMPORTANT.” Then she drew a heart with two arms. Karl looked at the drawing and said it was the most effective closing formula he had ever seen.

The letter left on a Monday morning. Viola wanted to post it herself, in the postbox in piazza Santo Spirito, standing on tiptoe. Then the waiting began. Every morning Viola asked Graziella whether the Crusca had answered. Every morning Graziella said no, and explained that academies are like ribollita: they need time. Meanwhile, following Bianca’s advice, everyone started using the word. First in the family: Giulia said Matei was abbraccioso on Sunday mornings, Matei said Lupino was abbraccioso with the customers who gave him bread. Then at the trattoria: Karl wrote “Ribollita abbracciosa” on the menu board, and customers began asking what it meant. Guido said his new slippers were abbracciosi, because they kept his feet warm. The fruit seller, after a week, declared that the July peaches were “abbracciose”, though nobody quite understood why. But the word was going around.

Not everyone was enthusiastic, though. One evening lawyer Bardi put down his fork and declared that inventing words was a way of ruining Italian. “The language of Dante,” he said, “doesn’t need a little girl’s inventions.” Silence fell over the trattoria. It was Bianca, who was helping at the tables that evening, who answered, with the calm of someone who has studied. She explained to the lawyer that Dante himself had been the greatest inventor of words in the Italian language. In the Comedy he had created verbs that didn’t exist before, like “trasumanar”, going beyond the human, or “imparadisare”, making like paradise, or “indiarsi”, becoming like God. He had made them with the same pieces Viola had used: a prefix, a root, an ending. “If Dante had waited for permission,” she concluded, “we would be speaking Latin today.” The lawyer was silent for a long moment. Then he laughed, raised his glass and said he surrendered. Before leaving, he ordered a ribollita abbracciosa to take home to his wife.

Meanwhile, at the Uffizi, the project went ahead. The first reproduction the group worked on was the Lippina itself, because Mr Alberto already knew it and could say whether the translation worked. Davide spent three weeks bent over the drawings, deciding what to keep and what to remove. The Madonna’s transparent veil had to be smoother than her dress. The angels had to have curly hair that fingers could recognise. The landscape in the background had to be lower than everything else, almost flat, to convey the distance. The relief-printing expert produced the prototypes with a special printer, and Mr Alberto touched them one after another, saying what he understood and what he didn’t. The first prototype was a disaster: too many lines, too many details. The second was better. The third finally worked. But they had to redo the relief of the angel’s face four times, because Mr Alberto said he couldn’t feel the smile.

The problem of the smile kept the group stuck for a week. How do you feel a smile with your fingers? The restorers proposed raising the corners of the mouth. The expert proposed a deeper line. Nothing worked: Mr Alberto touched and shook his head. Once again it was Davide who found the solution, but he didn’t find it at the museum: he found it at the trattoria, watching Viola hug Graziella. He noticed that when Viola smiled, she didn’t smile only with her mouth: her cheeks rose, her eyes narrowed, her whole face changed shape. The next day he proposed redoing not the mouth but the angel’s cheeks, making them fuller, rounder, higher. The expert printed the prototype. Mr Alberto touched it in silence, for a long time. Then he smiled too. “There he is,” he said. “The rascal. Now he’s laughing.” The project manager asked Davide how he had got the idea. Davide blushed. “From a huggy person,” he replied.

Meanwhile the Crusca’s reply didn’t come, and Viola was starting to worry. One evening, while Graziella was putting her to bed, she asked her whether words could die. Graziella sat on the edge of the bed and thought for a long time. Then she told her a secret she had never told anyone. Grandpa Aldo, she said, had invented a word too. In the evening, after service, when he was dead tired, he would sit on the kitchen stool and say: “Graziella, sono minestrato.” He meant tired and soft like a soup cooked too long. For forty years only the two of them had used it. When Aldo died, nobody said it any more. “So it died?” asked Viola, wide-eyed. Graziella smiled. “No,” she replied. “Because now you know it.” The next day, at eleven at night, Matei collapsed onto a chair after service and Viola, in her pyjamas on the stairs, shouted to him: “Daddy, you’re minestrato!” In the kitchen, Graziella had to lean on the table.

The Academy’s reply arrived after nineteen days, in a white envelope with the Crusca’s emblem, a frullone, that is, the old sieve used to separate flour from bran. It was addressed to “Viola, via Maggio, Florence”. Viola couldn’t read well yet, so she opened it in the kitchen, in front of everyone, and gave it to Pietro to read aloud. The letter was signed by a linguist of the Academy and was written with the same kindness as the “petaloso” letter. It said that the word “abbraccioso” was very beautiful and perfectly formed, with a noun and a suffix that have been used in Italian for centuries. It explained that similar words existed in some dialects, but not in standard Italian. And then it said a sentence Pietro had to read twice, because his voice was shaking: “Dear Viola, a word is like a hug: it’s worth nothing if you keep it to yourself. If you want it to enter the dictionary, you must give it to as many people as you can.”

When Pietro finished reading, nobody in the kitchen spoke. Viola was looking at him with a frown, as she did when she wasn’t sure she had understood. “So did they say yes or no?” she asked at last. Pietro looked for the right words. He explained that the Academy never says yes or no to a word, because it isn’t a judge: it’s more like a doctor who examines a newborn and says it is healthy. The word had been born well. Now it had to grow. And to grow it needed to be used, the way a child needs to eat. Viola thought about it, seriously. Then she announced that in that case the word needed a mother, and the mother was her. Giulia laughed until she cried. Matei said that in that house the grandchildren multiplied every month, now even those made of letters. Graziella took the letter and read it by herself with her glasses, slowly, moving her lips. Then she folded it in four and put it in her apron pocket, next to Aldo’s ribollita recipe.

Viola took the linguist’s advice very seriously. The next day, at the summer nursery, she taught the word to all her classmates, who took it home to their parents. On Sunday she taught it to don Paolo, who had come to lunch from San Leonardo, and he used it in the following Sunday’s homily, speaking of an “abbracciosa” Madonna with her child. Mr Alberto learned it at the Uffizi and repeated it to the whole working group. Ion, on the phone from Sibiu, learned it with a terrible accent and promised to teach it to his retired railway colleagues. Mancini, of course, wrote an article: “A little girl from via Maggio writes to the Crusca. The Crusca replies.” The article ended up in a national daily, then in a regional news programme, which sent a crew to the trattoria. In front of the camera, Viola said only: “Abbraccioso means you hug a lot. Try it.” Then she hugged the journalist, who was so surprised that he forgot to ask the next question.

The report was broadcast on a Tuesday evening, at a quarter to eight, and at the trattoria everyone stopped to watch it on the old television above the counter. It lasted two minutes. There was Viola with the Crusca’s letter in her hand, there was Graziella saying the word had been invented for her, there was Karl in front of the board with “Ribollita abbracciosa”, and at the end there was a linguistics professor from the university explaining, in simple words, how new words are formed in Italian. He said children are the best inventors of words, because they know the rules without knowing it and apply them without fear. He said “abbraccioso” was a perfect example of derivation, and that perhaps, in a few years, we would find it in the dictionary. When the report ended, the trattoria applauded. Viola, who had fallen asleep on Giulia’s lap halfway through, saw nothing. Graziella stroked her hair. “We’ll tell her tomorrow,” she said. “Tonight let’s let her sleep. Inventors are tired.”

In the following days something happened that nobody expected. The news report ended up on the internet, and the word started travelling on its own. A teacher from Palermo wrote to Mancini that her pupils had made a poster titled “The abbracciose people in our class”. A grandfather from Bolzano sent a postcard to the trattoria, addressed to the “abbracciosa grandmother of via Maggio”, with only this written on it: “My wife was too. Thank you for the word.” A singer-songwriter used it in a song that stayed in the charts for two weeks. A pastry maker from Bologna invented the “bacio abbraccioso”, a double chocolate, and sent a box to Viola, who shared it with the whole nursery. Bianca kept count on a sheet hung in the kitchen, like a researcher: every time someone used it outside the family, she added a tally mark. By the end of July there were more than two hundred marks. “It’s walking,” Bianca said, satisfied. “Now it doesn’t need us any more.”

That week, at home, Pietro and Bianca played a game. Bianca called it “the pieces game”: one said a word, the other had to take it apart into pieces and then put it back together in a new way. “Restauratore”: restaurare plus -tore, the one who restores. “Restaurabile”: that can be restored. “Irrestaurabile”: that can no longer be restored. “Ristrutturazione”: ri-, struttura, -zione. “Abbellimento”: a-, bello, -ire, -mento, the act of making beautiful. It was more fun than they had thought. Then they tried to invent new words, like Viola. Bianca proposed “ribollitaio”, the one who makes ribollita. Pietro proposed “domandoso”, someone who asks too many questions. Bianca laughed and said that word wasn’t needed, because there was already one: Pietro. Then they invented “guardabene”, a person who knows how to look, and “raccontastorie”, which already existed but seemed new to them. By the end of the evening they had a list of thirty words. They wrote them in the black notebook, under the title: “Dictionary of via Maggio. Volume one.”

A few days before the inauguration, Davide asked Pietro for help with a part of the project that scared him more than the relief: the audio description. Next to the reproduction there would be a button, and by pressing it the visitor would hear a voice describing the painting in three minutes. The museum guide had written a text, but Mr Alberto had listened to it and said it was “a shopping list”: too many names, too many dates, no emotion. Davide could draw, but he couldn’t write. Pietro could. They worked a whole night in Pietro’s room, with the black notebook open at the description of the Lippina that Pietro had written months before for school. Pietro wrote, Davide corrected: “Here the fingers feel the veil, say it first.” “Here’s the angel, make him arrive slowly, like a surprise.” At dawn they had a text of three hundred and twenty words. Mr Alberto listened to it the next day, recorded in Pietro’s voice. At the end he stayed silent. Then he said: “This isn’t a list. It’s a story.”

At the end of July, at the Uffizi, the project’s first reproduction was inaugurated. The Lippina in relief was mounted on a wooden lectern, next to the original, in the Filippo Lippi room, with a plaque in braille and in Italian. There were the museum director, the accessibility manager, the journalists, and the whole via Maggio family. Mr Alberto was the first to touch it in front of everyone. He touched the Madonna in profile, the smooth veil, the angels with curly hair, the low landscape in the background. Then he reached the angel’s face, with its full cheeks. He smiled. “The rascal is laughing,” he said. The room applauded. Then the director gave a short speech. He thanked the working group, Mr Alberto and “a young fifteen-year-old consultant who taught us that a touchable reproduction is not a copy, but a translation”. Davide went red to the roots of his hair. Rita, his mother, cried without shame. Viola, in Matei’s arms, shouted: “Davide is abbraccioso!” Everyone laughed.

After the ceremony, Mr Alberto asked to speak with Viola. He knelt in front of her, with his dog beside him, and asked her to teach him the word. Viola explained it to him with the seriousness of a teacher. Then, without asking permission, she hugged him. Mr Alberto stood motionless for a moment. Then he returned the hug, slowly. “You’re right,” he said with a trembling voice. “It’s a word you understand with your hands.” He stood up, leaned on his white cane and told Davide something that Davide wrote that very evening in his sketchbook, under a portrait of Mr Alberto with Viola. “For twenty years I thought I had lost my sight,” he said. “Today I understood that I had only lost my eyes. You gave me back my sight, with your hands.” Davide couldn’t answer. Rita put a hand on his shoulder. “You see,” she told him softly. “Now you know why this trade is worth doing.”

They all walked home together, crossing Ponte Vecchio in the orange light of the evening. Viola was asleep in Matei’s arms, with the heart with two arms drawn on the back of her hand. Davide walked ahead, in silence, with the project’s sample plaque under his arm, the one the director had given him. Halfway across the bridge he stopped and said to Pietro, without turning round: “I’ve decided. After high school I’ll study restoration at the Opificio. But I also want to do something else, something that doesn’t exist yet.” Pietro asked him what. Davide thought about it. “A restorer who doesn’t restore paintings,” he said. “He translates them. For those who can’t see them.” Pietro smiled. “Then you need a new word,” he said. “Restorer isn’t enough.” Davide shrugged. “You invent it,” he replied. “You’re the one with words.” Pietro thought about it for the rest of the bridge. By the time they reached via Maggio he had found it, but he decided to keep it to himself a little longer, like a gift to give at the right moment.

That evening, at the trattoria, Graziella did something she had never done in fifty years: she changed the name of a dish on the menu. On the board, under “Ribollita”, she wrote in chalk, in her crooked handwriting: “also known as abbracciosa”. Then she turned to the dining room and announced that from that day on anyone who ordered the ribollita abbracciosa would receive, along with the bowl, a hug from the cook. Free. The customers laughed. But that evening the ribollita ran out at half past nine, before any other dish, and Graziella hugged forty-seven people, including two Japanese tourists, a policeman and lawyer Bardi, who blushed like a little boy. Karl brought her the stool halfway through the evening, because Dr Neri had told her not to tire herself. Graziella refused it. “Hugs don’t tire you,” she said. “It’s the things you don’t do that tire you.”

Later, while they were closing, Karl told Pietro that in German new words are born in a different way. Germans, he said, don’t use suffixes much: they stick words onto each other, like the carriages of a train. A glove is a “shoe for the hand”, a fridge is a “cupboard of cold”. And you can build very long words that take up a whole line. Pietro asked him how he would translate “abbraccioso” into German. Karl thought for a long time, counting on his fingers. Then he said an eighteen-letter word that nobody managed to repeat and which, he explained, meant roughly “person who needs to hug”. Pietro laughed and said Italian was more practical. Karl shook his head. “Not more practical,” he said. “Different. German builds like an engineer: piece upon piece. Italian builds like a cook: it takes an ingredient and adds a flavour to it.” Pietro wrote the sentence in the black notebook, under Viola’s word, with an arrow that said: “See kitchen chapter.”

Before going to bed, Pietro opened the black notebook at the page of the “Dictionary of via Maggio” and added, at the top of the list, in red pen, the first word, the one that had given birth to all the others: “Abbraccioso, adj.: who hugs a lot. Coined by Viola Popa Esposito, six years old, July. Approved by the Accademia della Crusca (as a well-formed word). Awaiting entry into the dictionary.” Underneath he glued the linguist’s letter, and further down Viola’s drawing, the heart with two arms. Then he thought about it and added a footnote, as Ruggeri did in his articles: “Note: according to Grandma, hugs don’t tire you. According to Mr Alberto, they are understood with the hands. According to the Crusca, they’re worth nothing if you keep them to yourself. Three different sources, one conclusion.” He reread the note and smiled. It was the first time he had written a footnote. It seemed a grown-up thing to him. And, at the same time, the most childish thing in the world.
